prompt: What is a process model, according to the course text?

options.text: A graphical representation of how a business system should operate, showing its processes and how data move among them
A list of the organisation's employees
The physical layout of the servers
A table of the entities and their keys

explanation: A process model pictures the processes and the data moving between them.

why.a: Correct. That is the text's definition.
why.c: Wrong. That is a deployment view.
why.d: Wrong. That is the data model.

prompt: True or false: modelling the AS-IS system helps identify inefficiencies, delays or redundancies so that an improved TO-BE model can enhance performance.
explanation: Model today's system to find what is wrong, then model the improved one.

why.true: Correct. That is the text's reason for modelling as-is.
why.false: Wrong. The text says exactly this.

prompt: Match each term with its definition in the course text.

pairs.right: Activities producing a specific output for a customer or market; emphasises HOW work is done
Related activities in sequence with a beginning, an end, inputs and outputs: a structure for action
Organising and documenting processes, inputs, outputs and data stores; main tool the DFD

explanation: Four definitions that are easy to mix: a business process is about HOW, a process is a structured sequence, a model is a picture of reality, and process modelling documents it all with DFDs.

prompt: A business process emphasises HOW work is done. What does the course text contrast it with?

options.text: A product, which focuses on WHAT
A data store, which holds data at rest
An actor, which is outside the boundary
A class, which is a blueprint

explanation: Process is HOW; product is WHAT.

why.a: Correct. A product focuses on what.
why.b: Wrong. Data stores are DFD elements, not the contrast drawn here.
why.c: Wrong. Actors belong to use cases.
why.d: Wrong. Classes belong to object orientation.

prompt: What is the main tool of process modelling?

options.text: The Entity-Relationship Diagram
The Data Flow Diagram
The class diagram
The questionnaire

explanation: The DFD. The ERD is the data modelling tool.

why.a: Wrong. The ERD models data, not processes.
why.c: Wrong. The class diagram is object-oriented structure.

prompt: Which two of these are reasons the course text gives for the importance of process modelling?

options.text: It is cheap and easy to modify, especially with CASE tools
It shows exactly which programming language to use
Its non-technical notation is easily understood by business people
It removes the need for a data model

explanation: It focuses on business aspects, helps developers understand requirements, is cheap and easy to modify, is understood by business people, isolates parts at any level of detail, and documents how the business operates.

why.a: Correct. Cheap and easy to modify.
why.b: Wrong. DFDs contain no implementation details.
why.d: Wrong. The DFD and ERD together form the full picture.

prompt: According to the course text, what do DFDs allow the analyst to determine?

options.text: What the organisation does and how it does it
Which hardware the system needs
Who the shareholders are
How much each employee earns

explanation: A DFD shows data sources, the processes acting on the data, and the stores, so it reveals what the organisation does and how.

why.b: Wrong. DFDs carry no technical detail.
why.c: Wrong. Not what a DFD shows.
why.d: Wrong. Not what a DFD shows.

prompt: True or false: DFDs are physical models that include implementation details such as programming.
explanation: DFDs are purely LOGICAL. They are drawn first precisely because they are not contaminated by technical detail.

why.true: Wrong. DFDs are logical, with no implementation details.

prompt: Why does the course text say the DFD is drawn first?

options.text: Because it lets designers and users concentrate purely on the business aspects, without technical distractions
Because it is required by law
Because it contains the program code
Because it is the only diagram users can read

explanation: Logical and free of technical detail, the DFD keeps attention on the business.

why.d: Wrong. Use case narratives are also easy for users.

prompt: Match each DFD element with its symbol in the Gane-Sarson notation the course text uses.

pairs.right: An open-ended rectangle, two parallel lines

explanation: The four DFD elements and their symbols. Watch the two rectangles: square corners for an external entity, round edges for a process.

prompt: How many elements does a DFD have, and what are they?

options.text: Three: entity, attribute and relationship
Four: external entity, data flow, process and data store
Five: actor, use case, boundary, include and extend
Two: object and message

explanation: Four elements: external agent or entity, data flow, process, data store.

why.a: Wrong. Those are ERD elements (with identifiers, four).
why.c: Wrong. Those are use case diagram parts.
why.d: Wrong. Those belong to object interaction diagrams.

prompt: True or false: an external entity in a DFD performs processing on the data it sends.
explanation: An external entity is outside the boundary, the source and destination of data, and it does NOT perform processing. It is named with a singular noun.

why.true: Wrong. The text says external entities do not process.
why.false: Correct. External entities only send and receive.

prompt: How should a data flow be named, according to the course text?

options.text: With a verb, such as Calculate
With a noun that connotes the information, such as Order Details or Receipt
With the name of the programmer
With a number only

explanation: Data flows are pipes carrying packets of data, named with NOUNS that connote the information. Processes take verbs.

why.b: Correct. A noun naming the information.
why.c: Wrong. Not a naming rule in the text.

prompt: Which of these is a correctly named DFD PROCESS, by the course text's rules?

options.text: Add 1 to the counter
Student Master
Increment counter
Receipt

explanation: A process name contains a VERB and is NOT procedural. The text's own contrast: 'Add 1 to the counter' is procedural; 'Increment counter' is a process.

why.a: Wrong. The text gives this as a PROCEDURAL name, which is not allowed.
why.b: Wrong. That is a data store name.
why.c: Correct. A verb, and not procedural.
why.d: Wrong. That is a data flow name, a noun.

prompt: True or false: the data flowing out of a process has more value than the data flowing in, and a process is always active.
explanation: A process transforms input into output that is worth more after processing, and it is always active.

why.true: Correct. Both are in the text.

prompt: Which two of these are among the course text's hints that something is a logical PROCESS?

options.text: It makes decisions
It is a person outside the system
It creates, reads, updates or deletes a record
It holds data at rest

explanation: Hints: computes; decides; sorts, filters or summarises; organises data into information; triggers other processes; uses stored data (CRUD).

why.b: Wrong. That is an external entity.
why.d: Wrong. That is a data store.

prompt: What does the course text contrast a data store with, and how?

options.text: A data flow: the store is data at rest, the flow is data in motion
A process: the store computes, the process holds
An actor: the store is inside, the actor outside
An entity: the store is singular, the entity plural

explanation: Data at REST against data in MOTION. A store is drawn as two parallel lines and named without verbs, like Student Master.

why.a: Correct. At rest against in motion.
why.c: Wrong. Not the contrast the text draws.
why.d: Wrong. Not the contrast the text draws.

prompt: True or false: data store names should avoid verbs and physical descriptions of how the data is stored.
explanation: Names like Student Master or Client List, with no verbs and no physical detail.

why.true: Correct. That is the naming rule.
why.false: Wrong. The text states this rule.

prompt: Which notation is the DFD notation described in the course text, and which other notation does it mention?

options.text: Chen, with crow's foot as the alternative
Gane-Sarson, with DeMarco and Yourdon as the alternative
UML, with BPMN as the alternative
Scrum, with Kanban as the alternative

explanation: Gane-Sarson (rounded process rectangles); the other popular set is DeMarco and Yourdon.

why.a: Wrong. Chen and crow's foot are ERD notations.
why.b: Correct. Gane-Sarson, and DeMarco and Yourdon.
why.c: Wrong. Not what the text names for DFDs.

prompt: The iterative act of going from one single system to many component processes is called:

options.text: Balancing
Decomposition
Encapsulation
Conversion

explanation: Decomposition takes the analyst from a high-level overview down to detailed sub-processes, one level of abstraction at a time.

why.a: Wrong. Balancing conserves inputs and outputs across levels.
why.c: Wrong. Encapsulation hides an object's internals.

prompt: Match each DFD level with what it shows.

pairs.right: The whole system as ONE process, with external entities and flows; usually no data stores
All the major processes of the system, and it adds the data stores
Each process broken into sub-processes, such as Validate PIN, Check Balance, Dispense Cash

explanation: Context is one process; Level 0 shows the major processes and brings in the stores; Level 1 and below explode single processes. Every process model has exactly one Level 0.

prompt: True or false: a context diagram normally shows the system's own data stores.
explanation: Data stores are usually NOT included in a context diagram, unless they belong to other systems or processes. It shows only the external entities and the flows in and out of the single process.

why.true: Wrong. Stores are usually left out of the context diagram.
why.false: Correct. Stores first appear at Level 0.

prompt: How many Level 0 DFDs does every process model have?

options.text: Exactly one
One for each external entity
One for each data store
As many as there are processes

explanation: All process models have EXACTLY ONE Level 0 DFD.

why.b: Wrong. Entities do not multiply the Level 0.
why.c: Wrong. Stores do not multiply the Level 0.
why.d: Wrong. Processes are exploded into Level 1 diagrams, not Level 0s.

prompt: True or false: Level 1 and lower diagrams continue breaking processes down until each process is simple enough to understand.
explanation: Decomposition continues until the process is simple enough, as Withdraw Money breaks into Validate PIN, Check Balance and Dispense Cash.

why.true: Correct. That is when decomposition stops.
why.false: Wrong. The text says exactly this.

prompt: When decomposing a DFD you must conserve the inputs and outputs of the higher-level process. What is this called?

options.text: Decomposition
Balancing
Normalisation
Generalisation

explanation: Balancing ensures consistency across all levels: nothing appears from nowhere and nothing vanishes.

why.a: Wrong. Decomposition is the breaking down itself; balancing is the rule it must keep.
why.c: Wrong. Not a term in this unit.

prompt: True or false: in the course text's worked ATM example, the Customer is the only external entity on the context diagram.
explanation: The context diagram has the Customer alone; Level 0 then shows Authenticate User, Withdraw Money, Deposit Money and Check Balance, and Level 1 explodes Withdraw Money.

why.true: Correct. The Customer is the only entity.
why.false: Wrong. The example has only the Customer.

prompt: Match each DFD element with its naming rule.

pairs.right: A descriptive singular noun, such as Customer
A noun connoting the information, such as Order Details
Must contain a verb and must not be procedural
No verbs and no physical description, such as Client List

explanation: Only the process takes a verb. Entities, flows and stores are all nouns.

prompt: True or false: the course text describes a process as a specific ordering of work activities across time and place, with a beginning, an end, and clearly defined inputs and outputs.
explanation: A structure for action: inputs, actions, outputs, in sequence.

why.true: Correct. That is the text's definition.
why.false: Wrong. The text defines a process exactly so.
